claims.text: The as-synthesized refractory high-entropy alloy has a homogeneous single-phase microstructure.
The untreated alloy has high intrinsic strength.
The untreated alloy has limited ductility.
A controlled thermomechanical treatment involving cyclic heat treatment and subsequent deformation can nucleate nanoscale ductile precipitates.
The proposed treatment can produce a uniform dispersion of nanoscale ductile precipitates within the refractory matrix.
Intermediate processing temperatures and sub-critical deformation strains can favor fine-precipitate nucleation without coarsening.
An initial absence of large second-phase particles is a condition for the proposed treatment to produce the desired response.
Nanoscale ductile precipitates act as stress concentrators.
Precipitate-assisted localized plasticity and crack blunting lead to more uniform macroscopic deformation.
The refractory matrix retains high strength after the proposed precipitation treatment.
Maintaining the high-strength refractory phase preserves sufficient impact-induced energy release.
Relative to the untreated sample, the treatment increases ductility and reduces localized strain gradients.
The treatment largely maintains strength and impact-induced energy release relative to the untreated sample.
The hypothesis is limited to alloy compositions that can form suitable precipitates within the available processing window.
Slow precipitation kinetics or a tendency to form brittle intermetallics can prevent the proposed benefit.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant ductility or deformation-uniformity improvement without significant strength or energy-release loss would falsify the hypothesis.
